summary.text: A state of matter is one of the distinct forms matter can take, and four are seen in everyday life: solid, liquid, gas and plasma.
States differ in how their particles are arranged and behave together: packed in fixed spots in a solid, close but sliding in a liquid, far apart and free in a gas.
Beyond these four are many other states, such as liquid crystals, magnetic states, and Bose–Einstein condensates in extreme cold.

facts.label: Ice phases
facts.value: Fifteen known crystal structures at various temperatures and pressures

facts.label: Liquid crystals
facts.value: Show properties of both solids and liquids

facts.label: Iron's structures
facts.value: Body-centred cubic below 912 °C, then face-centred cubic

facts.label: Plasma
facts.value: Gas-like, plus charged particles that respond to electric and magnetic fields

items.prompt: You pour juice from a tall glass into a wide bowl. It takes the bowl's shape, yet the amount stays the same. What is going on among its particles?

options.label: They sit locked in fixed positions inside the bowl
They stay close together but slide past one another
They spread far apart to fill all the bowl's space
They become charged and respond to magnetic fields

items.explain: In a liquid the particles stay close but can move past one another, so the volume stays fixed while the shape follows the container.

items.prompt: A small puff of gas is released in one corner of a sealed room. What does it end up doing?

options.label: Spreading out until it fills the whole room
Staying in its corner with a clear edge
Settling into a thin layer on the floor
Keeping its own shape while drifting around

items.explain: A gas expands to fill the shape and volume of its container, so it occupies the entire room.

items.prompt: Water ice can form many different crystal structures at different pressures and temperatures. How do scientists classify these?

options.label: As different states, one for each crystal structure
As liquids that have only partly frozen
As different phases that all belong to the solid state
As forms of plasma created under pressure

items.explain: Ice is the solid state of water, yet it has multiple phases with different crystal structures, so one state can contain many phases.

items.prompt: A substance turns straight from a solid into a gas, never becoming a liquid on the way. Is that possible?

options.label: No, a solid must melt before it can boil
No, only liquids are able to become gases
Yes, but only after it first becomes a plasma
Yes, the process is called sublimation

items.explain: Solids can change directly into gases through sublimation, and gases can change directly into solids through deposition.

items.prompt: A coffee maker wants a dense, gas-like fluid that can dissolve caffeine out of beans. Which kind of substance fits?

options.label: A plasma produced by a huge voltage difference
A vapor liquefied by compression alone
A supercritical fluid above critical temperature and pressure
An ordinary gas held at low pressure

items.explain: A supercritical fluid has the properties of a gas but is dense enough to act as a solvent; supercritical carbon dioxide is used to extract caffeine.

items.prompt: A scientist wants to turn an ordinary gas into the electrically charged state. What could she do?

options.label: Cool it until its particles barely move
Run a huge voltage across it or heat it extremely hot
Compress it until it turns into a liquid
Let it expand into a much larger container

items.explain: A gas is usually converted to a plasma by a huge voltage difference between two points or by extremely high temperatures.
